To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cross-border loss-offset inherent to formula apptionment is a major hurdle for tax revenue neutrality and that the weight of input shares is crucial to the success of formula apportionment.

the short-term revenue losses through cross-border loss offset are not compensated by medium-term and long-term revenue gains, and that the extent of these losses is positively correlated with the probability of loss-making and negatively correlated with the costs of profit-shifting.
a switch from separate to formula apportionement decreases tax revenues and welfare in the short and medium run, but may be beneficial in the long run.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relevance of firm loss behavior for tax revenue and welfare effects when switching from separate to consolidated taxation.
the relevance of firm loss-making for tax revenues and the welfare of the tax base consolidation.
the question how the introduction of formula apportionment affects tax revenue losses due to cross-border loss offset and whether these losses are insurmountable for formula apportionment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tax revenue losses are not an insurmountable hurdle to formula apportionation, but the conditions under which this is the case are rather stringent.
a switch to formula apportionement would be beneficial in the long run only if the probability of loss-making firms is sufficiently low and if the costs of profit-shifting are sufficiently high.

a system change to formula apportionement is welfare improving in the long run if the probability of firms incurring losses is low and the costs of shifting profits are low or if the probability of losses is high but the costs of profit shiting are low or if both the costs of profit-shifting and the probability of losses are low.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cross-border loss offsets are the main reason for the lower tax revenues under formula apportionments.
tax revenues and welfare are unambiguously higher under separate accounting in the short run and under formula apportionation in the long run.
the tax revenue losses due to the crossborder loss offset inherent to a formula apportionment system are not insurmountable in the long run.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tax revenue losses in the short term may be a serious hurdle for the implementation of a formula apportionment system.

the cross-border loss-offset effect inherent to formula apaptionment may be a significant impediment to the adoption of formula apportionment, even if the formula is designed to mitigate tax competition.
the tax revenue losses through the cross-border loss-offset inherent to formula apaptionment cannot be overcome by the tax revenue gains from the elimination of double taxation.
